plain: Hi, and welcome!
Today we're going to learn how to hold a | pair of drumsticks the right way.
Don't worry if you've never | touched a drum before.
We'll go one step at a time, and by | the end of this video,
you'll be ready to play your | very first beat.
But first, a secret.
Most beginners hold their | sticks way too tight.
That one habit can hurt your sound, your | speed, and even your wrists.
So let's fix it from day one.
And stick around until the | end, pun intended,
because I've saved a bonus for you there.
All you need today is a pair of sticks.
If you're not sure which to buy, a size 5A | is the most common starting point.
It's not too thick, and not too thin.
You don't need a full drum kit yet.
A practice pad works great.
A firm pillow works too, if you | want to start right now.
Sit up straight, with your feet | flat on the floor,
and place your pad or pillow in front | of you at about waist height.
A drumstick has four parts.
The tip is the end that hits the drum.
Next is the shoulder, where the | stick starts to narrow.
The long middle part is the shaft.
And the end you hold is called the butt.
Remember that last one, because the | butt end is where we'll start.
Every stick has a balance point.
In drumming, we call it the fulcrum.
It's the spot where the stick feels | light and bouncy in your hand.
To find it, rest the stick across one finger | and slide it until it balances.
For most sticks, that's about a third of | the way up from the butt end.
Now pinch the stick at that spot,
between your thumb and the side | of your first finger.
Think of pinching a pencil, only lighter.
Just enough that it won't fall.
This pinch point is your pivot.
The stick swings around it, like a seesaw.
Quick check.
Can you wiggle the stick back | and forth freely?
If so, great.
If it feels stuck, you're | squeezing too hard.
Loosen up a little.
Now bring in your other fingers.
Curl your middle, ring, and pinky | fingers around the stick,
and let them rest there loosely.
A good way to picture it is | holding a small bird.
Firm enough that it won't fly away, and | soft enough that you won't hurt it.
Your fingers should touch the stick, | but not clamp down on it.
And the end of the stick should poke out | just a little past your palm.
Next, turn your hands so your palms | face down toward the drum.
Your thumbs should sit along the side of | the stick, not on top of it.
Bring the tips of the sticks close | together near the middle of the pad,
so they make a wide V shape.
This is called matched grip, because both | hands hold the stick the same way.
It's the most common grip, and a | great place to start.
Here's a fun test to see if | your grip is relaxed.
Hold the stick a few inches above | the pad, and let it drop.
Don't push it down.
Just let go of the lift and let | gravity do the work.
If your grip is loose, the stick will | bounce back up on its own.
That bounce is called rebound, and it's | what makes drumming feel easy.
If the stick just thuds and stops, | you're holding it too tight.
Relax your fingers and try again.
Once you can feel the bounce, try a few | slow taps with one hand at a time.
Let the stick do most of the work.
Let's look at five mistakes almost | every beginner makes.
Number one. The death grip.
Squeezing the stick as hard as you can.
The fix is to hold it like | that small bird.
Number two. Pressing your thumb | down on top of the stick.
Keep your thumb along the side, | and let it pinch lightly.
Number three. Holding the | stick at the very end.
This makes it wobbly and hard to control.
Go back to that balance point, | about a third of the way up.
Number four. Fingers sticking | out, away from the stick.
Keep them curled and resting on it.
And number five. Tense | shoulders and stiff wrists.
Take a breath, drop your shoulders, and | shake out your hands before you play.
Stick with me for one more | minute.
Your bonus is next.
You stuck around, so here's | your bonus: two last secret tips.
Tip one is your daily practice.
Set a timer for one minute.
Tap slowly, right, left, right, left, | and count one, two, one, two.
Keep everything loose, and listen | for that nice bounce.
Tip two: do this once a day, | not once a week.
A little every day beats one long session,
and your grip will start to | feel natural fast.
In the next video, we'll look at the drum | kit and what each piece does.
If this helped, subscribe, and I'll | see you in the next lesson.
